title: When a Number Won't Split Evenly
objective: Halving an odd number does not give two whole-number equal parts — an honest limit of the strategy, noticed and named without introducing formal fraction notation.
studentQuestion: Can this number be split into two exactly equal whole groups?
newIdea: Recognizing when a relationship (evenly halving) breaks down, and describing the leftover informally, without inventing fraction procedures.

teaching.setup: 7 counters; the learner is asked to split them into two equal groups.
teaching.see: Can you make the two groups exactly the same size?
teaching.break: Attempt the split — 3 and 3, with 1 left over that can't join either side evenly.
teaching.build: Describe the result honestly: 7 splits into 3, 3, and 1 left over — it doesn't split evenly in half.
teaching.transform: An even number's half (a clean whole-number answer) vs. an odd number's attempted half (two equal groups plus a leftover) — the value 7 is unchanged either way.

check.prompt: Recombine 3, 3, and 1 to confirm the total is still 7.

mastery.evidence: Correctly identifies whether a number up to 12 splits evenly in half, and if not, states the leftover, for 3 numbers.
